reason: Throughout this Exodus narrative, Moses and Aaron are consistently portrayed as faithful instruments of God's will, following divine instructions to lead the Hebrew people out of Egypt. The text repeatedly shows the people themselves murmuring and complaining despite God's provision: they lament the loss of Egyptian comfort (16:2-3), doubt God's presence (17:2-7), and fear when facing the Egyptian army (14:11-12). The text attributes the people's difficulties primarily to external oppression (Pharaoh's hardened heart), their own lack of faith, and God's sovereign plan—not to leadership failure. Moses and Aaron are shown faithfully executing God's commands, performing miracles, and maintaining their authority even when the people express doubt. The narrative framework suggests that the leaders' conduct is righteous and divinely mandated.
